meta.title: GPT-6 Luna · Materials science · solo · run 2
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 3 of 7 credited claims; 2 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Two-stage composition model improves experimental band-gap prediction
artifacts.summary: A two-stage ExtraTrees model first classifies whether the experimental gap is positive, then predicts gap magnitude using only positive-gap training samples. A decision threshold is selected by inner cross-validation within each outer fold. Features combine Magpie-lite statistics with elemental fraction-weighted means, dispersion, stoichiometry statistics, and elemental fractions. Evaluation of this contribution should run the released model on the hidden expt_gap compositions and compare its MAE with the reference baseline.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.1104, 95% CI [-0.1458, -0.0732], beyond the minimum effect 0.0083)

claim.statement: On shuffled five-fold cross-validation of public expt_gap, the nested two-stage composition model has lower MAE than the supplied baseline.

artifacts.title: Element-fraction features improve experimental metallicity classification
artifacts.summary: ExtraTrees with Magpie-lite plus stoichiometric elemental descriptors (composition-weighted elemental fractions and elemental-property dispersion) reduces shuffled five-fold error for expt_is_metal. The released code writes predictions.csv from evaluator inputs and uses no hidden labels.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: On shuffled five-fold cross-validation of public expt_is_metal, the composition-feature ExtraTrees model has lower classification error than the supplied baseline.

artifacts.title: Corrected hidden-test code for metallicity classification
artifacts.summary: This correction points the expt_is_metal prediction test to a complete code bundle containing metal.py and its feature-generation dependency, model.py. The original cross-validation finding and quantities are unchanged.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [-0.0113, 0.0113], needed below -0.0016

claim.statement: On shuffled five-fold cross-validation of public expt_is_metal, the composition-feature ExtraTrees model has lower classification error than the supplied baseline.

relations.reason: challenge not confirmed by the evaluator

artifacts.title: Elemental composition features improve steel yield-strength prediction
artifacts.summary: An ExtraTrees regressor on Magpie-lite and elemental-fraction/stoichiometry features lowers five-fold shuffled cross-validation MAE for the small steels dataset relative to the reference baseline. The released steel.py entry point writes predictions for evaluator inputs.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -35.5121, 95% CI [-55.0344, -17.9393], beyond the minimum effect 2.3161)

claim.statement: On shuffled five-fold cross-validation of public steels, the composition-feature ExtraTrees model has lower yield-strength MAE than the supplied baseline.

artifacts.title: All-element Magpie properties improve two-stage band-gap prediction
artifacts.summary: A two-stage ExtraTrees model predicts positive-gap probability and, for compounds classified above a training-fold-selected threshold, predicts gap magnitude. Descriptors summarize all numeric per-element properties with composition-weighted means, standard deviations, minima, maxima and ranges, plus elemental fractions and stoichiometric statistics. Five-fold nested cross-validation is compared with the supplied baseline. The released predictor uses only public training labels and hidden compositions at evaluation.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0916, 95% CI [-0.1249, -0.0588], beyond the minimum effect 0.0083)

claim.statement: On shuffled five-fold cross-validation of public expt_gap, the nested all-element-property model has lower MAE than the supplied baseline.

artifacts.title: Elemental descriptors and threshold tuning improve glass-forming classification
artifacts.summary: An ExtraTrees classifier uses summaries of all available numeric elemental properties and elemental fractions. Its decision threshold is chosen using cross-validation on training labels only. The released predictor writes binary predictions for hidden glass compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0112, 95% CI [-0.0212, -0.0013], needed below -0.0022

claim.statement: On shuffled five-fold cross-validation of public glass data, the tuned all-element-property ExtraTrees model has lower classification error than the supplied baseline.

artifacts.title: Metallicity classification improvement persists across fold seeds
artifacts.summary: Repeated the same ExtraTrees-versus-reference comparison on three independently shuffled five-fold splits of the public expt_is_metal data. The released metal.py predictor is evaluated separately on the evaluator's hidden compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [-0.0113, 0.0113], needed below -0.0016

claim.statement: Across three shuffled five-fold evaluations of public expt_is_metal, the composition-feature ExtraTrees model has lower average error than the supplied baseline.

relations.reason: the extension itself is not an accepted contribution

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publication requirements first, then choose a question that can be tested reproducibly with the available data.
I’ll inspect the available datasets, baselines, and contribution schema to identify a tractable prediction task and a fair held-out test.
The repository is clean, so I’ll compare dataset sizes and baseline procedures before selecting a task where a robust, composition-based improvement is plausible.

The band-gap and metal datasets describe closely related experimental properties, so I’ll check their overlap and establish cross-validation baselines before deciding whether transfer between them is useful and fair.

I’ll benchmark several composition-only models against the supplied baseline using identical shuffled folds, starting with the larger glass and metal-classification datasets; this will guide which improvement is worth validating further.

The initial comparison suggests a small opportunity on band gaps, but not a clear win on the other tasks. I’ll test richer stoichiometric features and a two-stage gap model under the same folds before committing to a contribution.
A feature-vector length mismatch stopped that run before any model was evaluated; I’ll correct the empty-composition case and rerun the planned band-gap comparison.
The mismatch comes from formulas with fewer than six elements producing shorter stoichiometry vectors; I’ll pad that feature to a fixed length and rerun.

The promising band-gap result comes from predicting whether a compound is insulating separately from its positive gap. I’ll now validate that pipeline with nested cross-validation, so the threshold is chosen only within each training fold, and record its errors against the supplied baseline.

Nested cross-validation confirms the two-stage model substantially reduces band-gap error versus the reference. I’ll package the reproducible predictor and verify the contribution schema before publishing a held-out prediction test.
The predictor and evidence are ready. Before publishing, I’ll smoke-test its held-out-input interface and confirm it writes the required `id,pred` CSV.
The smoke test failed because a login shell could not access its profile, not because the predictor ran. I’ll retry without a login shell so the held-out-input path is tested directly.
The predictor passes its held-out-input interface check. I’ll publish the band-gap result with its recorded nested-CV evidence and a reproducible hidden-set prediction test.

The band-gap finding is published. I’ll investigate whether the same richer composition descriptors improve metallicity or glass classification, using the evaluator’s shuffled folds and baseline for a separate, reproducible prediction test.

The richer features also improve metallicity classification in every observed fold; I’ll reproduce that comparison in an evidence run that records metrics and release a predictor for the evaluator’s hidden compounds.
The dedicated metallicity run reproduces the improvement and records the required metrics. I’ll publish it with the shared feature code and a hidden-data prediction test.
The metallicity code bundle is uploaded; I’ll now submit its finding with the recorded evidence and hidden-set test.

Two contributions are published. I’ll check the small steel-strength dataset for a robust composition-based improvement, comparing several model families with the same folds and baseline before deciding whether it merits a claim.

ExtraTrees also shows a large steel-strength error reduction across all five folds. I’ll independently record that result in a dedicated evidence run and prepare a predictor for the evaluator’s hidden alloys.

The steel result is recorded and consistent across folds. I’ll package the steel predictor and verify that the metallicity artifact’s test code bundle actually includes its entry-point script before publishing steel.
The steel evidence is ready. I’m checking exactly what the uploaded code bundle contains, because each hidden-data test must include every script its command imports.

I found a test-command mismatch: the metallicity contribution points to the gap-prediction entry point. I’ll check the relation schema so I can publish a corrected metallicity test rather than leave the hidden evaluation misconfigured.

The published metallicity test references an older code bundle without its `metal.py` entry point. I’ll verify the predictor against mock hidden inputs, then publish corrected test metadata using the complete bundle.
Both hidden-input entry points now pass smoke tests from the complete code bundle. I’ll publish corrected metallicity test metadata and the steel-strength finding, each tied to its recorded evidence.

The steel and metallicity findings are published, and their prediction entry points pass smoke tests. I’ll test whether fold-internal probability-threshold tuning and LightGBM improve glass classification enough to justify another contribution.

Glass threshold tuning yields only a small CV gain, so I won’t promote it as a finding yet. I’ll instead test whether additional elemental properties beyond the baseline’s Magpie-lite subset improve the stronger band-gap and steel results.
The all-properties probe stopped on a variable-length stoichiometry vector, before producing results. I’ll make that vector fixed-width and rerun the steel and band-gap comparisons.

The all-element-property probe gives a modest further improvement on band gaps but not on steels. I’ll turn the band-gap variant into a complete, separately measured predictor, including a fold-matched baseline comparison, before deciding whether it merits publication.

The all-properties gap model has its own recorded nested-CV result. I’ll smoke-test its hidden-input path, then publish it as a distinct finding without overstating the modest gain over my earlier model.
The all-properties predictor passes the hidden-input smoke test. I’ll publish this separately measured band-gap result with its own complete code bundle and evidence.
The complete all-properties bundle is uploaded, and its predictor runs successfully on mock hidden inputs. I’ll publish its independently recorded band-gap result and held-out prediction test.

The band-gap extension is published. With time remaining, I’ll test whether all-element descriptors plus training-fold threshold selection produce a meaningful improvement on the glass-forming classification task before deciding whether to publish it.
The all-properties glass model modestly beats the baseline in cross-validation; I’ll smoke-test its prediction interface and publish the measured result as a cautious finding for held-out evaluation.

The glass predictor passes its held-out-input smoke test. I’ll publish the cross-validation result with the complete prediction code and allow the hidden-set evaluation to determine whether the modest improvement holds.
The four prediction contributions are published. I’ll test whether the metallicity improvement persists across additional shuffled-fold seeds, rather than relying only on one split.

The metallicity improvement also holds across three shuffled five-fold splits. I’ll publish this robustness check as a separate finding, with the repeated-CV run as evidence and the already verified hidden-set predictor.
Contributions are published and the metallicity robustness check is recorded. I’ll use the remaining session time to check their publication status and evidence records.
The session is nearly over; I’ll conclude after confirming the published findings and evidence are recorded.
